analysis.one_liner: Caps interest and fees on consumer credit at 36% a year.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee, dying without a hearing, a vote, or any action after its April 2019 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a national 36% annual cap into federal law on what any lender can charge a consumer, counting not just the interest rate but late fees, overdraft fees, cash advance fees, and add-on products. It would have applied to payday loans, car title loans, overdraft programs, and high-rate credit cards alike, and let state attorneys general and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's existing framework enforce it. Violating lenders could face prison time and fines, and loans made above the cap would be unenforceable in court.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who currently pay triple-digit rates: the bill's own findings estimate consumers pay roughly $14 billion a year on overdraft loans, up to $7 billion on payday loans, and $3.8 billion on car title loans, at average annual rates near 400% for payday loans and 300% for car title loans. People carrying high-rate credit card balances would also be capped, and borrowers could void loans made above the limit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Payday, car title, and high-rate card borrowers

how_it_helps.text: Sets a single national maximum of 36% including all fees, closing the loopholes and state-law exemptions the bill's findings say let high-cost lending persist in all 50 states.

Makes any loan exceeding the cap unenforceable: the lender must return all principal, interest, and fees, and the borrower can raise the violation as a defense at any time, even during collection or repossession.
Adds enforcement teeth: criminal penalties of one year in prison and a fine of up to three times the accrued debt or $50,000 per violation, plus state attorneys general can sue in federal court.
Requires billing statements to show the all-in 'fee and interest rate' as 'FAIR' instead of a conventional APR, so borrowers see the true cost including fees.

analysis.who_pays: Payday, car title, and online installment lenders would lose their core business model, which the bill's findings put at roughly $11 billion a year in storefront and title lending alone. Banks and card issuers would lose overdraft, late-fee, cash-advance, and high-interest-card revenue. Some borrowers with poor credit might lose access to small-dollar credit altogether, since lenders below 36% may not find it profitable to serve them.

drawbacks.text: A 36% cap can price some borrowers out of credit entirely: lenders cannot profitably make small, short-term loans to high-risk borrowers below that rate, so people who today use payday or car title loans might be left with no formal option in an emergency. The bill acknowledges this by calling for alternatives like low-fee installment loans, but it does not create them.

The cap sweeps in ordinary credit card and bank fees, including late fees and overdraft charges, so banks and issuers would have to reprice products that millions of borrowers who never pay triple-digit rates also rely on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people currently paying 300% to 400% annual rates, the benefit is large and direct, and the bill's own findings put those costs at over $20 billion a year across overdraft, payday, and title lending. The real cost is that some borrowers who cannot qualify for cheaper credit may lose access to any small-dollar loan; whether that is an acceptable trade is the honest disagreement over usury caps. The bill also has a strong enforcement design (void loans, criminal penalties, state AG suits), but its breadth, covering every credit card fee, is what makes industry opposition inevitable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never held a hearing or a vote on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on April 29, 2019, joined by Senators Merkley, Blumenthal, and Whitehouse.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote in the remainder of the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday, car title, and online installment lenders keep charging rates the bill's findings put near 400% a year, and banks keep collecting overdraft, late, and high-interest credit card revenue that a 36% cap would have curtailed. Borrowers paying those rates are no better off than before.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it as lead sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Jeff Merkley, Richard Blumenthal, and Sheldon Whitehouse
for.role: U.S. Senators (D-OR, D-CT, D-RI), original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other senators signed on during the Congress.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs (Republican-chaired)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress: no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Payday, car title, and installment lenders and banking/card industry
against.role: Industries whose revenue the 36% cap would cut
against.what_they_did: Opposed a national 36% rate cap, which would eliminate most high-cost small-dollar lending and cut overdraft and card fee revenue.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the Republican majority that controlled the Banking Committee and the Senate calendar never acted on it.

industries.industry: Payday, car title, and online installment lenders
industries.note: The bill's findings put their combined annual take at roughly $11 billion from storefront payday and title loans alone, at average rates near 400% and 300%. A 36% all-in cap including fees would end the product as it exists, which is the point of the bill.

The cap counts overdraft fees, late fees, cash advance fees, and add-on products toward the 36% limit, cutting revenue streams the bill's findings value at roughly $14 billion a year for overdraft alone. Lenders below the cap lose little; the highest-rate card products and fee-heavy accounts are hit hardest.
Loans above the cap become void and unenforceable, so collectors could not pursue or repossess on them, but ordinary sub-36% debt is untouched.
